topics.label: Lecture introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic frames the lecture within the cancer course and introduces its learning objectives.

topics.label: Cancer evolution and the origins of cancer-driving mutations
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations arise and enable clonal evolution toward cancer within a permissive microenvironment.

topics.label: Environmental cancer risks and evidence for their contribution
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the evidence and uncertainty surrounding environmental contributions to cancer rather than attributing it solely to chance or inherited predisposition.

topics.label: Infectious causes of cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections contribute to cancer, with Burkitt lymphoma illustrating cooperation between pathogens and cellular changes.

topics.label: Environmental carcinogens and mechanisms of DNA damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental exposures produce DNA damage and mutations through mechanisms shaped by their chemical properties and metabolism.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish mutation-producing initiation from promotion that enables altered cells to proliferate in a supportive environment.

topics.label: Tissue and developmental susceptibility, with a recap of carcinogenic mechanisms
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain context-dependent susceptibility to carcinogens and conclude by placing it within the preceding account of cancer-causing mechanisms.

topics.label: Methods for identifying exposures and assessing carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how evidence of carcinogen exposure and cancer-causing potential can be obtained, interpreted and limited.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit perspective
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic closes the lecture by summarising its conclusions and framing everyday exposure decisions as risk–benefit judgments.
